                    4K LAND AND CATTLE COMPANY’S
          REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION


I.   Introduction

       4K Land and Cattle Company (“4K Land”) files this Reply to Exceptions pursuant to 16
TAC § 22.261 and respectfully requests that the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(“Commission”) adopt the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued by the Administrative Law
Judges (“ALJs”) in its entirety. The PFD recommends denial of the Certificate of Convenience
and Necessity (“CCN”) application filed by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA
Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, “Applicants”) for a 765-kV high-voltage
transmission line that would traverse the properties of 4K Land and hundreds of other Texas
landowners. That recommendation to deny is well-supported by the evidentiary record and should
be affirmed.

       In supporting the ALJs’ recommendation that the CCN application be denied, 4K Land’s
primary submission is that Applicants failed to carry their statutory burden under PURA § 37.056
to demonstrate that the proposed project is necessary, convenient, or useful to accommodate
legitimate public demand. 4K Land does, however, except to the PFD’s contingent finding that, if
the Commission were to grant any CCN, Route 894 should be selected. As set forth herein and in


4K Land and Cattle Co. Reply Exceptions to the PFD
PUC Docket No. 59475; SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                    Page 3
   4K Land’s prior Exceptions, the evidentiary record compels adoption of a Northern Corridor route
  (including Route 410, Route 416, or Route 392) should the Commission choose to approve a route.

            The exceptions filed by Applicants, Commission Staff, and a few other parties ask the
  Commission to override the ALJs’ factual findings and grant a CCN that the record plainly does
  not support. Applicants’ Exceptions essentially argue that House Bill 5066 (HB 5066) and the
  Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) automatically establish need – a legal theory squarely
  rejected by the ALJs’ analysis and proposed Findings of Fact (“FOFs”). 1

            This Reply addresses the exceptions in the order in which the PFD treats the issues.
  Throughout this Reply, 4K Land respectfully submits that the Commission should give appropriate
  weight to the ALJs’ credibility determinations and their careful assessment of the evidentiary
  record, which spans thousands of pages of written testimony, exhibits, and hearing transcripts.


VII.      Need (Issues 5-7)
            PURA § 37.056(a) requires that an applicant for a CCN demonstrate that the requested
  certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. This
  burden rests squarely on the applicant, and the Commission may not presume necessity from an
  ERCOT planning recommendation or a legislative transmission planning directive. The ALJs
  correctly applied this standard in evaluating Applicants’ evidence of need, and their conclusion
  that Applicants failed to carry their burden is fully supported by the record.

            HB 5066 (codified at PURA § 39.167) is a planning directive that instructed ERCOT to
  develop a transmission plan for the Permian Basin region. It is not a construction mandate, and it
  did not make any finding of project-specific need for any particular transmission line. Critically,
  unlike the CREZ legislation (PURA § 39.904), which expressly exempted CREZ transmission
  projects from the conventional necessity showing under PURA § 37.056, HB 5066 contains no
  such exemption. Projects arising from HB 5066 planning must therefore satisfy the full PURA §
  37.056 standard. This distinction – which Applicants ignore – is the foundation of the ALJs’ need
  analysis, 2 and it is legally correct.

  PUC Docket No. 59475; SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                      Page 4
            Applicants’ Exceptions argue that the ALJs erred by not according “great weight” to
ERCOT’s recommendation in the PBRP. This argument fundamentally misconceives the
Commission’s role under PURA § 37.056. Even if ERCOT’s recommendation were entitled to
“great weight” under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), the Commission is still required to make
an independent determination that the proposed transmission facility “is necessary for the service,
accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.” The “great weight” standard is not a
presumption of need; it does not relieve Applicants of their evidentiary burden; and it does not
authorize the Commission to approve a CCN application on the basis of a planning document
alone. PURA § 37.056(a) requires the Commission to find necessity based on the evidence
presented in the CCN proceeding. That evidence must include the “historical load, forecasted load
growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection [. . .]” as PURA § 37.056(c-1)
specifies. Moreover, under the “great weight” subsection in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), the
forecasted load growth and additional load seeking interconnection must be “substantiated by
quantifiable evidence.” In this case, the ALJs correctly found no such quantifiable evidence.

           A. HB 5066

           Applicants’ Exceptions devote substantial attention to the proposition that HB 5066
(PURA § 39.167) establishes project-level need for the proposed 765-kV transmission line. 3 That
argument is legally incorrect and was properly rejected by the ALJs. 4 HB 5066 directed ERCOT
to develop a long-range transmission plan for the Permian Basin region; it made no finding that
any specific transmission project is necessary, convenient, or appropriate. The statute is a planning
directive, not a construction mandate, and it cannot substitute for the applicant-specific necessity
showing required by PURA § 37.056(a).

           The contrast with the CREZ legislation is decisive. PURA § 39.904 expressly provided
that CREZ projects were “necessary for the public interest” and exempted them from the
conventional CCN necessity showing. The Legislature knew how to write a statutory necessity
finding when it wanted to. HB 5066 contains no such language. It provides no project-specific
determinations, no route authorizations, and no exemption from § 37.056. Applicants’ attempt to

PUC Docket No. 59475; SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                        Page 5
 read a CREZ-type exemption into HB 5066 by implication has no textual basis and should be
rejected. The ALJs’ conclusion 5 that HB 5066 “directed ERCOT to develop a plan” but did not
“make a finding of need for each project” is a legally sound interpretation of the statute and should
be adopted by the Commission. 6

           B. The Permian Basin Reliability Plan

           The PBRP is the product of ERCOT’s HB 5066 planning exercise. Applicants’ Exceptions
and Staff’s Exceptions 7 argue that the PBRP’s inclusion of Import Path 2 – the general
transmission corridor of which the proposed project is an element – establishes project-specific
need. That argument misunderstands both the nature of the PBRP and the Commission’s prior
treatment of it. As the PFD 8 correctly states, the Commission approved the PBRP as a planning
document but expressly reserved individual CCN proceedings for the project-level necessity
determination. The PBRP is the starting point for the analysis, not the conclusion.

           More fundamentally, the PBRP’s load forecasts – the factual foundation on which
Applicants’ need case entirely rests – are unreliable. The ALJs found that ERCOT’s
recommendation should not receive “great weight” in this proceeding because the underlying load
forecasts upon which it is based have been materially undermined by subsequent events, including
ERCOT’s own realization-rate methodology adjustments, the failure of oil-and-gas electrification
projections to materialize, and the passage of Senate Bill 6. As Intervenor Howton’s Exceptions
correctly observed, “great weight is conditional” – the condition being that the forecasted load
growth and additional load currently seeking interconnection are “substantiated by quantifiable
evidence of projected load growth.” The condition failed here because “ERCOT made no finding
in the PBRP that it deemed the S&P Global load forecasts credible.” An ERCOT recommendation
is only as reliable as the data supporting it; where that data is demonstrably flawed, according it
“great weight” would be arbitrary. Witness Marusak’s testimony acknowledged that the

           DBM’s Exceptions argue that the PBRP enjoys a presumption of validity that its opponents
failed to rebut. 9 That argument overstates the PBRP’s legal status and misallocates the burden of
proof. It is Applicants’ burden under PURA § 37.056 to demonstrate necessity; it is not an
intervenor’s burden to disprove a planning document. As the PFD correctly recognized, “HB 5066
does not make a transmission project’s inclusion in a reliability plan a finding that the project is
needed. The necessity for any transmission project included in the PBRP must be independently
determined by the Commission through the lens of PURA § 37.056.” Moreover, the record
evidence introduced by intervenors and ERCOT’s own post-PBRP methodological revisions
collectively rebut any presumption that the PBRP’s load forecasts remain valid. As the PFD lays
out, ample evidence regarding the S&P Global study and the realization-rate methodology provide
a robust evidentiary basis for the ALJs’ finding that the PBRP’s load projections are unreliable.

           C. Changed Circumstances

                    1. ERCOT’s Adjusted Load-Forecasting Methodology
           The PFD’s findings document one of the most significant factual developments in this
record: after the PBRP was finalized and after Applicants filed their CCN application, ERCOT
adopted new realization-rate discount factors that substantially reduce the projected value of large-
load interconnection requests. Specifically, ERCOT applied a 55.4% realization-rate discount to
officer-letter loads and a 49.8% discount to data-center loads. 10 When these discounts are applied
to the PBRP’s non-oil-and-gas projected load, the projected demand is reduced by at least 3,571
MW. 11 This reduction is not trivial: Import Path 2’s safe loading limit is approximately 5,270
MW. 12 A 3,571 MW reduction in the non-oil-and-gas load component alone eliminates most of
the headroom that the PBRP projected would require the full build-out of Import Path 2. The
Commission should not approve a multi-billion-dollar transmission project whose need case rests

 on load forecasts that ERCOT’s own subsequent methodology demonstrates were materially

           Applicants’ Exceptions argue that ERCOT’s realization-rate adjustments are irrelevant
because they postdate the PBRP and because need analysis should be based on the conditions that
existed when the project was conceived. 13 That argument is both practically and legally untenable.
The Commission must base its CCN determination on current conditions and current evidence, not
on a snapshot of projected conditions that the record now shows to have been overstated. The very
purpose of ERCOT’s realization-rate methodology was to address the recognized risk that load
forecasts based on officer letters and interconnection queue data systematically overstate actual
demand. As the Commission explained when approving the methodology, the concern was that
accepting unreliable load forecasts may result in an overestimation of load growth and an overbuild
of transmission.

                    2. Senate Bill 6
           The PFD’s findings address 14 the enactment of Senate Bill 6 (SB 6), which establishes new
credibility standards for large-load interconnection requests. SB 6 requires entities seeking large-
load interconnections to demonstrate financial capability, provide deposits, and meet other
threshold criteria before their load projections may be used in transmission planning. The load
projections that underlie the PBRP were developed before SB 6 was enacted and predate its
credibility requirements. Until SB 6 is fully implemented and until the loads that depend on it have
satisfied its standards, those projections should not be treated as reliable inputs for infrastructure
planning decisions of the magnitude proposed in this proceeding.

           Applicants’ Exceptions do not meaningfully engage with the SB 6 findings. Applicants
note that SB 6 postdates the PBRP but offer no explanation for why loads that fail SB 6’s credibility
standards should nonetheless support a multi-billion-dollar transmission commitment. Witness
Poole’s testimony regarding the historical pattern of large-load interconnection requests that do
not ultimately materialize 15 provides important context: the PBRP’s load projections represent
aspirational demands from entities that had not yet demonstrated the financial or operational

                   3. Import Path 2’s Purpose Under Generation Adequacy
           The PFD’s findings address a critical gap in Applicants’ need case: even if Import Path 2’s
rated capacity were needed to serve projected load growth in the data-center corridor, Applicants
failed to identify the specific generation resources that would supply the power to be transmitted
through that path. 16 This omission is fundamental because Import Path 2’s stated purpose is to
enable westward power flow from central Texas to the Permian Basin. Applicants’ witnesses
described Import Path 2 as essential for westward power export from the Bell County East hub,
but provided no sensitivity analysis demonstrating whether central Texas generation can
simultaneously serve the growing local data-center loads in that area and export sufficient volumes
westward to justify the full capacity of the proposed 765-kV line.

           The finding that Applicants failed to identify the specific generation resources that would
supply Import Path 2’s capacity is, as the ALJs observe, devastating to Applicants’ case:
Applicants failed to show that the grid can supply the power that Import Path 2 is designed to
transmit. Without this showing, the capacity of the proposed line cannot be tied to any identifiable
generation resource or any demonstrated grid need. Applicants’ witnesses testified regarding
ERCOT’s aggregate capacity projections, but their testimony did not perform the disaggregated
analysis necessary to show that Bell County East specifically will have sufficient generation to fill
Import Path 2’s capacity. As the PFD found, “[n]either Oncor nor ERCOT studies parse out central
Texas’s net generation position under any scenario: current conditions, projected conditions in
2030, nor projected conditions in 2038 assuming 50 percent of queued large load interconnection
requests in that region materialize.” 17 The ALJs correctly identified this failure as independently
fatal to Applicants’ need case.

            D. The ALJs’ Analysis of Need

                    1. Considering the Forecasted Loads
           The PFD’s findings examine the load forecasts on which Applicants’ need case depends.
The oil-and-gas electrification projections were based entirely on the S&P Global study
commissioned by ERCOT. That study was the sole basis for the oil-and-gas load forecast
incorporated into the PBRP; no independent corroboration was offered. Critically, the S&P Global
study relied heavily on non-binding corporate pledges from Permian Basin operators to electrify
their operations – pledges that, as the record subsequently demonstrated, operators have not
honored and have in many cases abandoned. 18 Notably, ERCOT itself commissioned an
independent academic study from the Bureau of Economic Geology at the University of Texas at
Austin, which projected oil-and-gas-related load reaching only 3.1 GW by 2030 – compared to the
S&P Global figure of 10.3 GW for 2030. 19 The PBRP adopted the industry-submitted S&P Global
number and did not reconcile or even acknowledge this independently commissioned academic
study. Applicants have offered no satisfactory explanation for that omission.

                    2. Projected Non-Oil and Gas Load
           The PFD’s findings address the non-oil-and-gas load component of the PBRP
projections. 20 At the time the PBRP was developed, approximately 59% of the projected non-oil-
and-gas load in the relevant transmission zone was classified as cryptocurrency mining load.
Crypto mining is notoriously volatile and price-sensitive; it tends to curtail or relocate rapidly in
response to changes in electricity prices, regulatory conditions, or cryptocurrency valuations. By
the time of the evidentiary hearing, the load mix in the affected zone had shifted dramatically
toward data-center load, with crypto mining representing a substantially smaller share of the total.
The ALJs found 21 that this compositional shift, combined with the realization-rate discounts
applicable to data-center loads, further undermines the PBRP load projections as a basis for
assessing current transmission need.

                      3. Projected Oil and Gas Load
           The PFD’s findings address what the ALJs characterized as the core evidentiary failure of
the oil-and-gas load projections: the S&P Global study’s central premise – that Permian Basin
operators would electrify their field operations at the rates projected – has been proven incorrect
by subsequent events. The record shows that major Permian operators have, in fact, reduced their
emissions without electrifying their operations, primarily through operational efficiency
improvements, fuel switching at individual facilities, and other measures that do not require
connection to the ERCOT grid. The S&P Global study, which was developed by S&P Global and
submitted to ERCOT by Oncor, incorporated industry-provided projections that have proven
unreliable.

                     4. Far West Import GTCs
           The PFD’s findings address Applicants’ reliance on Generic Transmission Constraint
(“GTC”) data from Far West Texas import paths. Applicants argue that the GTCs demonstrate
binding transmission constraints that Import Path 2 would relieve, thereby validating the need for
the proposed project. The ALJs correctly recognized that GTCs measure the existence of
transmission constraints, not the composition or reliability of the loads that are driving those
constraints. A GTC that is being triggered by crypto-mining load that has since curtailed or
relocated does not establish a durable need for new transmission capacity. As intervenor evidence
demonstrated, the PBRP reflected that mainly datacenter/crypto load constituted a substantial
portion of the additional non-oil-and-gas load, with ERCOT’s own observation that the total
amount of additional non-oil & gas load is almost the same as the oil & gas load. 22 The GTC data
cannot validate PBRP load forecasts because it does not independently confirm the nature,
longevity, or location of the loads that produced the constraints.

                     5. Bell County East Cannot Supply Power
           These findings are significant because they identify a logical gap at the center of
Applicants’ need case. 23 Import Path 2 is predicated on a large volume of generation being
available at or near Bell County East to flow westward through the proposed 765-kV line. But
Applicants did not identify the specific generation resources that would supply that power.

 Applicants’ testimony references “central Texas generation” in aggregate terms, but performs no
disaggregated analysis of whether the specific resources in or near Bell County East have sufficient
capacity to simultaneously serve the growing local data-center loads in that area and export
westward at the volumes Import Path 2 was designed to carry.

                   6. Independent Need for Import Path 2
           The PFD’s findings address whether a partial build-out of Import Path 2 – rather than the
full 765-kV project proposed by Applicants – could address any legitimate near-term transmission
need. 24Applicants conducted no partial-build analysis. They offered no testimony regarding
whether a lower-voltage solution, a shorter segment, or a phased approach could address any
demonstrated constraint without imposing the full scale and cost of the proposed project on
affected landowners and Texas ratepayers. The absence of a partial-build study is particularly
significant because the record contains evidence that near-term transmission needs in the corridor,
to the extent they exist at all, may be addressable through solutions substantially smaller than the
proposed 765-kV line. Additionally, the PFD reflects the ALJs’ finding that the need for the project
in the 2030 timeframe – the earliest date by which construction could realistically be completed –
has not been established on the current record. 25

                   7. Weight to ERCOT’s Recommendation
           The PFD’s findings address the weight that should be accorded to ERCOT’s
recommendation in favor of the proposed project. 26 Applicants and Staff both argue that ERCOT’s
recommendation as the independent system operator should receive substantial deference. The
ALJs disagreed, finding that ERCOT’s recommendation does not warrant “great weight” in this
proceeding because the underlying data on which it was based is demonstrably unreliable. 27 This
is the correct approach. Deference to an agency recommendation is calibrated to the quality of the
data supporting it; where, as here, the forecast inputs have been undermined by ERCOT’s own
subsequent methodology revisions, the passage of SB 6, and the actual behavior of Permian Basin

           The evidence revealed that ERCOT’s recommendation was developed using the pre-
realization-rate methodology and that ERCOT had not updated its recommendation to reflect either
its own subsequent methodology changes or the actual realization of the loads that were the
primary driver of projected need. An ERCOT recommendation developed based on data that
ERCOT itself has since revised is not a sufficient basis to support a project of this magnitude.

                    8. New Gas Generation in Permian Basin
           The PFD’s findings document the substantial new gas-fired generation being planned and
developed in the Permian Basin region. 28 The record identifies 37 new gas generation projects
totaling approximately 39.467 GW of proposed capacity in or near the Permian Basin. This figure
rivals or exceeds the total PBRP-projected load for the entire Import Path 2 corridor. The
development of local Permian Basin generation at this scale is directly relevant to Import Path 2’s
need case because it suggests that the region may, over the relevant planning horizon, develop
sufficient local generation capacity to serve its own load growth without requiring large-scale
westward import of power from Bell County East. If Permian Basin load can be served by local
generation, the transmission constraint that Import Path 2 is designed to relieve may not materialize
as projected.

           Applicants’ Exceptions do not seriously engage with the new-gas-generation evidence.
Applicants argue that new generation projects frequently do not reach commercial operation and
that the Commission should not rely on projects that are still in the planning stage. But this
argument applies with equal or greater force to Applicants’ own load projections, which are based
on even more speculative corporate commitments. Texas operates a competitive generation
market, and neither the Commission nor ERCOT has authority to order generation to be built at a
particular location or to guarantee its output for the Import Path 2 Projects. Similarly, however,
neither can the Commission order loads to materialize that have been forecast on the basis of
unverified officer letters and corporate pledges. 29 The asymmetry in Applicants’ position is

                   9. Conclusion on Need
           The ALJs’ findings on need represent the culmination of their analysis. 30 The first finds
that Applicants failed to carry their burden of demonstrating that the proposed 765-kV
transmission line is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public
within the meaning of PURA § 37.056(a). 31 The second finds that, given the cumulative weight of
the changed circumstances – ERCOT’s realization-rate methodology revisions, the failure of oil-
and-gas electrification projections, SB 6, and the development of new Permian Basin generation –
the CCN application should be denied. 32 These findings are fully supported by the evidentiary
record and represent a reasonable, well-articulated exercise of the Commission’s fact-finding
authority.

           Applicants’ request that the Commission substitute its own assessment of the evidence for
the ALJs’ considered findings should be denied. The ALJs presided over the evidentiary hearings,
assessed the credibility of numerous witnesses, reviewed thousands of pages of testimony and
exhibits, and produced a detailed PFD grounded in specific record citations. The PFD’s
conclusions of law correctly state that “ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation is not entitled to great
weight in the determination of need for this reliability project” under 16 TAC §
25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), and that “[t]he evidence does not establish that amendment of Applicants’
respective CCNs is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
public” under PURA § 37.056. 33 The Commission should give appropriate weight to those
determinations. To the extent the Commission has any doubt regarding the need findings, the
appropriate response is to require Applicants to refile with updated load data that incorporates
ERCOT’s revised realization-rate methodology, reflects SB 6 credibility requirements, and
accounts for actual rather than projected Permian Basin electrification rates. The Commission
should not grant a CCN for a project whose need has not been demonstrated on the current record.

           For these reasons, 4K Land respectfully requests that the Commission adopt the PFD’s

          J. Prudent Avoidance


          The Commission' s prudent avoidance policy, codified at 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(6) and
 (b)(3)(B)(iv), requires that transmission lines conform, to the extent practicable, to a policy of
 limiting exposures to electric and magnetic fields ("EMF") that can be avoided with reasonable
 investments of money and effort. Prudent avoidance is achieved primarily by minimizing the
 number of habitable structures located in close proximity to the route and by maximizing distance
 from those structures where feasible. 49
         Route 894' s supporters treat the habitable-structure count as a proxy for prudent-avoidance
 compliance, and on that metric Route 894 performs well at 85 structures within 500 feet. But
 prudent avoidance is not limited to a single numerical count. It encompasses a broader principle
 of minimizing exposure that can be avoided with reasonable expenditures. Here, the relevant
 inquiry is whether the incremental cost of a Northern Corridor route represents a "reasonable
 investment of money and effort" to avoid the concentrated ranch-operation, environmental,
 aesthetic, and community-values impacts that Route 894 imposes. For a proj ect whose total
 estimated cost exceeds $1.68 billion, a cost differential of 2.04% to 3.38% is a reasonable
 investment to secure materially better performance on every non-habitable-structure routing factor.
          The Commission should not allow a narrow habitable-structure advantage - based on data
 the Applicants' own witness was prepared to revise - to override the multi-factor analysis that
 PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require.
